flashcards.q: Rank iterrows(), .apply(axis=1), and vectorised operations by speed, roughly.
flashcards.a: Vectorised fastest (single-digit to tens of ms at ~1M rows); .apply() typically 50-100x slower; iterrows() slowest, commonly 100-700x slower than vectorised, because it constructs a full Series object per row.

flashcards.q: Why does a Series of ints with one missing value become dtype float64?
flashcards.a: NumPy's int64 has no bit pattern for missing values, so pandas silently upcasts the whole column to float64 (which supports NaN) the moment any value is missing.

flashcards.q: What pandas dtype avoids the int-to-float64 NaN promotion, and how?
flashcards.a: The nullable Int64 dtype (capital I) — it represents missing values via pd.NA internally without requiring a float upcast.

agg reduces each group to a scalar (one row per group). transform returns the same shape as the input, broadcasting each group's result back to every row in that group. filter keeps or drops whole groups based on a predicate, returning a subset of original rows.

flashcards.q: What does merge(..., validate='one_to_many') check, and what does it catch?
flashcards.a: It verifies keys are unique on the left side before merging, raising MergeError immediately if not. It catches the bug where an assumed cardinality is silently violated by a duplicate key introduced upstream, which would otherwise multiply output rows with no error.

flashcards.q: What caused SettingWithCopyWarning, and what changed about it in pandas 3.0 (Jan 2026)?
flashcards.a: Whether df[mask] returned a view or a copy was an undocumented, layout-dependent implementation detail, so chained assignment could silently work or not work. Pandas 3.0 made Copy-on-Write the only mode: every operation behaves as an independent copy, SettingWithCopyWarning is removed, and chained assignment now raises an explicit error instead of warning.

flashcards.q: What's the correct one-step fix for chained assignment like df[mask]['col'] = value?
flashcards.a: df.loc[mask, 'col'] = value — a single, explicit, labeled assignment instead of two chained indexing operations.

flashcards.q: Outline the pandas approach to expanding (start_date, end_date) rows into one row per month.
flashcards.a: Per row, build a list of month-start timestamps with pd.date_range(start, end, freq='MS'), store it in a column, then call df.explode(that_column) to turn each row's list into separate output rows. Guard against ranges within a single month, which produce an empty list and silently vanish under explode.

flashcards.q: Give the SQL equivalent of the date-range-to-month-rows expansion.
flashcards.a: generate_series(date_trunc('month', start), date_trunc('month', end), interval '1 month') joined per row (Postgres/DuckDB), or a JOIN against a pre-populated calendar table filtered with BETWEEN start and end month for engines without generate_series.

resample changes the index's frequency (fewer or more rows, calendar-aligned) — e.g. daily to weekly sums. rolling keeps the same row count and computes a sliding-window statistic, by default windowing over a fixed number of ROWS, not calendar time.

flashcards.q: Why can rolling(window=7) on a datetime-indexed series with a gap give a misleading result, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: By default rolling windows by row count, not elapsed time, so a gap in the index means the last 7 rows span more than 7 calendar days. Fix: use a time-based window string, rolling('7D'), which windows by actual elapsed time.

flashcards.q: When does the category dtype help, and when does it not?
flashcards.a: It helps on low-cardinality columns (status flags, country codes) by storing unique values once plus small integer codes per row. It doesn't help — and adds overhead — on high-cardinality/mostly-unique columns like UUIDs or free text.

flashcards.q: Roughly what dataset size threshold marks the point to move from pandas to Polars, and from a single machine to PySpark?
flashcards.a: Pandas is comfortable under roughly 1GB / a few hundred million cells on one machine; above that, Polars (multi-threaded, lazy) is the modern default. PySpark's community-validated threshold is roughly 10B+ rows / 10+TB requiring genuinely multi-machine, distributed joins.

flashcards.q: Why does pivot() raise ValueError on duplicate (index, columns) pairs, and what's the fix?
flashcards.a: pivot requires a unique combination of index and columns values to place each value unambiguously; duplicates raise. Use pivot_table instead, which accepts an aggregation function (default mean) to resolve duplicates.
